verified.notes: Checked 16 Nov 2026 (checker agent on Fable; 62 blocks, option labels, prompts and the four diagram panels; Livy lat3 and lat2, Roberts, Polybius grc2 and Pleiades opened). Every Latin and Greek quotation matched. Fixed 8 errors and 11 lesser points with the checker's wording, without a second pass: the 'together' option made counterfactual (the council decided the opposite, 10.27.2); Polybius' Gallic quarrel is 2.19.2–3; the apparatus at 10.29.7 and Roberts at 10.28.8 described as they stand; the Umbrians of Livy's second version are beaten in the end (10.26.12); the Gauls were solicited for pay, not recorded as paid (10.18.2, 10.21.2); an uncited date for Polybius cut; the diagram caption names every drawn element that is ours; footer raised to 20 px. Not opened, so left out: Duris in Diodorus 21.6, Frontinus 1.8.3, the Fasti Triumphales, Zonaras, Dio. Not yet checked. Researcher's draft notes (2026-11-16). Livy cited by the Conway–Walters (OCT) section numbers in Perseus lat3; 10.29.7, 10.29.18 and 10.30.5 compared with Weissenborn–Müller (lat2). Roberts 1912 (Perseus eng3) is not quoted: his section numbers run differently from the OCT in 10.26–10.31, he prints Niebuhr's 1,000,000 at 10.30.5, renders 'iterum longius evectos' (10.28.8) as 'a third charge' and Madvig's 'peditum' as cavalry, and is loose at 10.27.11 and 10.31.14; English is ours throughout. Two of his footnotes are cited as his (on the Umbrians, at 10.27.10; on the repeated shield-wall, at 10.29.11). Perseus OCR and layout fixes in quoted Latin: 'certamen certarnen' (10.27.3), duplicate removed; the OCT margin 'A.U.C. 459' removed (10.27.4, 10.31.14); apparatus notes interleaved in the text removed (10.28.17 'contacturum s: contracturum W.'; 10.30.5 the note on 'sexiens centena milia'); 'inquit' omitted from the quotation of 10.28.13 and marked with an ellipsis. Polybius from Perseus grc2 (tlg0543.tlg001), line breaks closed up; the section numbers 2.19.1–6 were counted from the file's paragraph divisions and should be confirmed. Pleiades from isawnyu/pleiades.datasets data/gis/places.csv (413312 Sentinum, 413060 Camerinum, 413096 Clusium, 413004 Ager Gallicus); pleiades.stoa.org not opened. Years BC are the conventional ones; Livy's sequence of consular years (295 Fabius–Decius, 294 Postumius–Atilius at 10.32.1, then Papirius at 10.38.1) is the basis for 'two years later'. Not found or not reachable, so not used: Frontinus, Strategemata 1.8.3 (not in PerseusDL canonical-latinLit); Diodorus 21.6 with Duris' figure for the dead (Perseus has no text of book 21); the Fasti Triumphales entry for 295 (no edition opened); Zonaras, Cassius Dio, Orosius, Accius' Decius; Livy, Periocha 11 (so the end of the war in 290 is not stated). A Commons photograph of the Civitalba frieze was found (File:Fregio del tempio di Civitalba - Museo Archeologico Nazionale delle Marche.jpg) but not used: it is a scan from a 1991 magazine under PD-Italy, flagged on Commons as requiring review, and its record describes Celts fleeing a plundered temple without connecting it to Sentinum. Oakley vol. IV and Walbank not opened; no modern study is cited. blocks.text: The territory of Sentinum, 295 BC. Four peoples are in arms against Rome here: Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians. Gellius Egnatius commands your Samnites.

The consuls Q. Fabius and P. Decius have crossed the Apennines and camped about four miles from you. They bring four legions, a strong Roman cavalry, a thousand picked Campanian horse, and an army of allies and Latins larger than the Roman. Two more Roman armies stand facing Etruria, not far from Rome, in Faliscan and in Vatican land.
blocks.note: The figures are Livy's. The manuscripts have transgresso Appennino, the consuls crossing; the Oxford text and Weissenborn–Müller print Gronovius' transgressos, which makes the enemy the ones who had crossed.

blocks.text: Before the consuls came, a Roman force was beaten. One account puts it at Clusium, where the Senones surrounded a legion; some say not a man was left to carry the news, others that the attackers were Umbrians, the loss small, and the Umbrians beaten in the end. Another account puts it in the land of the Camertes and gives the victory to Samnites and Gauls together.
blocks.note: See the card Clusium or the Camertes.

blocks.text: The leaders of the four peoples are in council.
The game seats you among the elders of the touto with Gellius Egnatius' army, whose counsel he asks.

steps.prompt: The four peoples must settle how to camp and how to fight the consuls. What do you advise?

options.label: Two camps and two tasks. We and the Gauls give battle; while it is fought, the Etruscans and Umbrians attack the Roman camp.

consequence.text: The council agrees on just this, and a day is fixed.

quote.la: ita convenit ne unis castris miscerentur omnes neve in aciem descenderent simul; Samnitibus Galli, Etruscis Umbri adiecti. dies indicta pugnae; Samniti Gallisque delegata pugna; inter ipsum certamen Etrusci Umbrique iussi castra Romana oppugnare.
quote.en: It was agreed that they should not all be mixed in one camp, nor go down into line together; the Gauls were joined to the Samnites, the Umbrians to the Etruscans. A day was fixed for the battle; the fighting was assigned to the Samnite and the Gauls; during the fight itself the Etruscans and Umbrians were ordered to attack the Roman camp.
quote.it: Si convenne che non si mescolassero tutti in un solo accampamento e che non scendessero in campo insieme; ai Sanniti furono aggiunti i Galli, agli Etruschi gli Umbri. Fu fissato il giorno della battaglia; il combattimento fu affidato al Sannita e ai Galli; durante lo scontro stesso gli Etruschi e gli Umbri ebbero l'ordine di assalire l'accampamento romano.

consequence.note: Perseus prints 'certamen certarnen'; the duplicate is removed. 'Samniti' is a collective singular. The English is ours.

consequence.text: Then three men of Clusium slip out by night and cross to the consul Fabius.

options.label: Keep all four peoples on the field and fight the consuls together.
options.kind_note: No one is recorded proposing this; some writers put all four at the battle

consequence.text: In some writers the Umbrians and Etruscans too are present at the battle. They give the enemy host a number of foot that is corrupt in the manuscripts and that editors restore as hundreds of thousands or a million, with forty-six thousand horse and a thousand wagons, and add the proconsul L. Volumnius and his army to the Roman side.
consequence.note: See the card The number Livy laughed at.

consequence.text: The historian who reports them says they have overshot belief. In most annals the victory belongs to the two consuls alone. The account that reports this has the battle fought without the Etruscans and Umbrians.
What four peoples in one line would have done, no source can tell us.

options.label: Fix no day. Hold the camps, refuse battle and let the consuls wear themselves out so far from home.
options.kind_note: No one is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: The Gauls were courted with money: their help was sought for pay, and at Rome the price was reported as huge.

In one account, a few years before this, Gauls who had raided Roman land through Etruria came home safe with their plunder, quarrelled over the shares, and destroyed most of the plunder and of their own force.
consequence.note: Polybius dates the battles of 295 'in the fourth year' after this raid (2.19.5).

consequence.text: Whether a host sought with money would have sat and waited, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: The council agreed on two camps: Samnites and Gauls to fight the battle on a fixed day, Etruscans and Umbrians to attack the Roman camp during it. Some writers, whom Livy rejects, had all four peoples at the battle.

blocks.text: Three deserters from Clusium crossed to Fabius secretly by night and gave away the plan. They were sent back with gifts, to bring word of each new decision as it was made.
The consuls wrote to Cn. Fulvius in Faliscan land and L. Postumius in Vatican land: move your armies up to Clusium and lay the enemy's country waste with all your force.

quote.la: huius populationis fama Etruscos ex agro Sentinate ad suos fines tuendos movit. instare inde consules, ut absentibus iis pugnaretur.
quote.en: The report of this ravaging moved the Etruscans from the territory of Sentinum to defend their own borders. The consuls then pressed to have the battle fought while they were away.
quote.it: La notizia di questa devastazione mosse gli Etruschi dal territorio di Sentino a difendere i propri confini. I consoli allora incalzarono perché si combattesse in loro assenza.

blocks.text: Livy names only the Etruscans as marching off. Yet a few lines later he writes of the battle as fought without the Etruscans and the Umbrians. He does not say where the Umbrians had gone; Roberts, translating in 1912, noted that the surviving authorities give no answer.
Polybius has none of this. In his short account Samnites and Gauls fight the Romans alone; he names no Etruscans or Umbrians in that year, no council and no deserters.
The Etruscans have marched home to defend their own land.

The consuls are pressing for a battle while they are away. For two days the Romans have come out to provoke you. Nothing worth telling has been done; a few have fallen on each side, and tempers are roused for a real fight.

steps.prompt: The Etruscans are gone and the consuls offer battle. What should Gellius Egnatius and the Gauls do?

options.label: Go down into the plain with everything we have.
options.kind_note: What the Samnites and Gauls did

consequence.text: On the third day both sides go down into the plain with all their forces. The Gauls take the right, you the left. Facing you is Fabius with the first and third legions; facing the Gauls, Decius with the fifth and sixth.
A later judgement on the first clash:

quote.la: primo concursu adeo aequis viribus gesta res est ut si adfuissent Etrusci et Umbri, aut in acie aut in castris, quocumque se inclinassent accipienda clades fuerit.
quote.en: At the first clash the fight was so even that, had the Etruscans and Umbrians been there, in the line or at the camp, wherever they had thrown their weight a defeat would have had to be accepted.
quote.it: Al primo urto si combatté con forze così pari che, se fossero stati presenti Etruschi e Umbri, in linea o all'accampamento, dovunque si fossero volti si sarebbe dovuta subire una sconfitta.

consequence.note: The judgement is Livy's own. He does not write 'by the Romans', but the defeat he means is theirs. The English is ours.

options.label: Stay behind the rampart. Send after the Etruscans, and fight when they are back.
options.kind_note: No one is recorded proposing this

consequence.text: A battle without the Etruscans is exactly what the consuls are pressing for.

In Etruria in these same days Fulvius does great damage to the fields and also fights a battle: more than three thousand men of Perusia and Clusium are reported killed, and about twenty standards taken.
Whether the Etruscans would have come back, or the Gauls waited for them, no source can tell us.

outcome.text: On the third day both sides went down into the plain with all their forces: Gauls on the right against Decius, Samnites on the left against Fabius. Livy judged that with the Etruscans and Umbrians present the first clash would have gone against Rome.

blocks.text: Livy tells it wing by wing. Against the Gauls, Decius spent his strength at once. His horse twice drove off the Gallic cavalry; carried too far, it was scattered by armed men riding in on chariots and wagons, and the rout broke the legions' front. When he could not stop it, Decius called on his father by name. The words given to him:

quote.la: quid ultra moror … familiare fatum? datum hoc nostro generi est ut luendis periculis publicis piacula simus. iam ego mecum hostium legiones mactandas Telluri ac dis Manibus dabo.
quote.en: Why do I put off any longer the fate of my house? It is given to our family to be the offerings that pay for the dangers of the state. Now I will give the legions of the enemy, with myself, to be sacrificed to Tellus and the di Manes.
quote.it: Perché indugio ancora davanti al destino della mia famiglia? Alla nostra stirpe è dato di essere vittime espiatorie per scongiurare i pericoli pubblici. Ora offrirò con me le legioni dei nemici, da immolare alla Terra e agli dèi Mani.

blocks.note: 'inquit' is omitted at the ellipsis. The English is ours.

blocks.text: The pontifex M. Livius spoke the formula before him; Decius rode where the Gauls stood thickest and was killed. The Romans rallied. The Gauls closed up behind their shields.

Against you, Fabius held his men back and dragged out the day. He was convinced that Samnites and Gauls are fierce in the first onset and need only be withstood, and that in a longer fight the Samnites' spirit sinks. When your shout, your charges and your missiles had lost their force, he sent his horse round to your flank, moved his line forward, and then threw in every reserve. Your line did not hold. It ran past the Gallic line to the camp and left the Gauls fighting.

The battle as Livy tells it, in four panels: the lines, with the hind and the wolf between them; Decius' wing, the chariots and the devotio; the Gallic shield-wall and Fabius' attack; the camp and the Gallic rear. A diagram of his words, not a plan of the field. Ours: the orientation and every distance; the place of the Samnite camp, put behind the Gallic wing because Livy has the Samnites run past the Gallic line to reach it; the order of the two legions within each wing; the side on which the horse rides round; and where on the Gallic front Decius rode in. Also ours: the number of blocks in each line and their equal size; the Gallic horse drawn behind its own foot once driven off; the side from which the chariots come; the Roman horse drawn in front of the Gallic foot, where Livy puts it in among them; and the line of Decius' legions still facing the Gauls in the last panel, of which Livy says nothing at that point. The legion numbers and the figure of about 500 Campanian horse are Livy's.

figure.alt: Diagram in four numbered panels. One: Gauls on the right wing face Decius with legions five and six; Samnites on the left wing face Fabius with legions one and three and reserves behind; between the lines a hind turns to the Gauls and a wolf to the Romans; a Samnite camp behind. Two: Gallic horse driven off, Roman horse among the Gallic foot, chariots coming on, the Roman front disordered, and Decius riding into the Gallic line. Three: the Gauls in a block behind their shields with javelins thrown at them and reserves arriving; Fabius' horse on the Samnite flank, his legions advancing, the Samnites fleeing past the Gallic line to the camp. Four: Fabius at the camp, a cross where Gellius Egnatius falls, and the Campanian horse with the principes of the third legion coming round behind the Gauls.

blocks.text: Hearing that his colleague was dead, Fabius sent the Campanian horse, about five hundred, round behind the Gauls, with the principes of the third legion to follow. He vowed a temple and the spoils to Jupiter Victor and went on to your camp.

quote.la: ibi Gellius Egnatius, imperator Samnitium, cecidit. compulsi deinde intra vallum Samnites parvoque certamine capta castra et Galli ab tergo circumventi.
quote.en: There Gellius Egnatius, the commander of the Samnites, fell. The Samnites were then driven inside the rampart, the camp was taken after a short fight, and the Gauls were surrounded from the rear.
quote.it: Lì cadde Gellio Egnazio, comandante dei Sanniti. I Sanniti furono poi ricacciati dentro il vallo, l'accampamento fu preso con breve combattimento e i Galli furono circondati alle spalle.

blocks.note: 'There' is under the rampart itself, where those shut out by the crowded gates turned to fight (10.29.15).

blocks.text: Livy gives 25,000 of the enemy killed and 8,000 taken, and on the Roman side 7,000 dead from Decius' army and 1,700 from Fabius'. Polybius gives no figures: the Romans killed most of them and drove the rest to flee, each to his own country.
blocks.note: The 1,700 is an old correction; the manuscripts are corrupt at this point. See the card The number Livy laughed at.

blocks.text: A Samnite column of five thousand, fleeing through the land of the Paeligni, was surrounded by them and lost about a thousand. Fabius triumphed over Gauls, Etruscans and Samnites.

Samnium did not make peace. In the same year Samnites came down to plunder the land of Vescia and Formiae, and that of Aesernia and along the Volturnus. Their legions were brought to battle in the Stellate plain; Livy gives 16,300 killed and 2,700 taken, and 2,700 Roman dead.
Livy stops his narrative here to say what he thinks of your people.

quote.la: nec suis nec externis viribus iam stare poterant; tamen bello non abstinebant. adeo ne infeliciter quidem defensae libertatis taedebat et vinci quam non temptare victoriam malebant.
quote.en: They could no longer stand either by their own strength or by that of others; yet they did not hold back from war. So far were they from wearying of a liberty defended even without success; they preferred to be beaten rather than not to try for victory.
quote.it: Non potevano più reggersi né con le forze proprie né con quelle altrui; eppure non si astenevano dalla guerra. A tal punto non si stancavano della libertà, pur difesa senza fortuna, e preferivano essere vinti piuttosto che non tentare la vittoria.

blocks.note: The OCT margin 'A.U.C. 459', interleaved in the Perseus text, is removed. The English is ours.

blocks.text: Two years later a levy was held through all Samnium under an old rite of oath, and about forty thousand men, the strength of Samnium, mustered at Aquilonia. Livy gives 20,340 killed there in a day. The end of the war lies beyond the passages opened for this scene.
blocks.note: Some manuscripts give sixty thousand for the muster (10.38.4, apparatus). Livy's consular years: Postumius and Atilius follow Fabius and Decius (10.32.1), then L. Papirius Cursor (10.38.1).

blocks.text: Livy closes his account by rebuking writers who inflated the battle.

quote.la: Magna eius diei quo in Sentinati agro bellatum fama est, etiam vero stanti; sed superiecere quidam augendo fidem, qui in hostium exercitu peditum sexiens centena milia, equitum sex et quadraginta milia, mille carpentorum scripsere fuisse, scilicet cum Umbris Tuscisque, quos et ipsos pugnae adfuisse
quote.en: Great is the fame of the day on which the battle was fought in the territory of Sentinum, even for one who keeps to the truth; but some have overshot belief by exaggeration, writing that in the enemy's army there were six hundred thousand foot, forty-six thousand horse and a thousand wagons, counting, of course, the Umbrians and Etruscans, who by their account were also present at the battle.
quote.it: Grande è la fama del giorno in cui si combatté nel territorio di Sentino, anche per chi si attiene al vero; ma alcuni, esagerando, hanno oltrepassato il credibile, scrivendo che nell'esercito nemico c'erano seicentomila fanti, quarantaseimila cavalieri e mille carri, s'intende con gli Umbri e gli Etruschi, che secondo loro presero parte anch'essi alla battaglia.

blocks.note: Oxford text (Conway–Walters) as in Perseus, with the apparatus note removed. 'Six hundred thousand' is Walters' conjecture; see the next block.

blocks.text: The figure for the foot is not what the manuscripts give. The Oxford apparatus reports x.cccxxx in one manuscript and xl.cccxxx in others, with one hand writing out forty thousand three hundred and thirty. Walters printed sexiens centena milia, six hundred thousand; the apparatus records Niebuhr's deciens centena milia, a million. Weissenborn and Müller print milia trecenta triginta, 330,000. Roberts translated a million.
So the number Livy calls beyond belief is itself lost: 40,330 foot would be no exaggeration beside 46,000 horse, and each editor has restored a figure large enough to earn the rebuke.
blocks.note: Our inference from the apparatus; no commentary was opened.

blocks.text: The same writers added the proconsul Volumnius and his army to the consuls' legions. In most annals, Livy says, the victory belongs to the two consuls, while Volumnius in Samnium drives a Samnite army onto the Tifernus mountain and routs it. His own battle order agrees: the second and fourth legions were with Volumnius in Samnium.
Livy's own Roman losses have a doubtful numeral too. Fabius' 1,700 dead rest on a correction, septingenti; the apparatus shows the manuscripts corrupt here, and a later reading gives ducenti, 1,200.

Livy has Fabius leave the second legion at Clusium, "which they once called Camars", under L. Scipio as propraetor. Before the consuls arrived, Senones in great numbers came to attack it. Scipio led his men up a hill between the town and the camp without scouting the way; the enemy already held the ridge, and the legion was cut down from behind and surrounded.

Livy then reports two versions. Some authorities say the legion was destroyed so completely that no one survived to report it, and that the consuls learned of it only when Gallic horsemen came in sight with heads hung on their horses' chests and fixed on their lances, chanting in their fashion. Others say the enemy were Umbrians and the loss smaller: foragers under the legate L. Manlius Torquatus were surrounded, Scipio brought help from the camp, and the Umbrians were beaten and stripped of prisoners and plunder. Livy thinks Gauls the likelier, because fear of a Gallic rising gripped Rome that year.
Polybius gives two sentences.

quote.la: μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα πάλιν ἔτει τετάρτῳ συμφρονήσαντες ἅμα Σαυνῖται καὶ Γαλάται παρετάξαντο Ῥωμαίοις ἐν τῇ Καμερτίων χώρᾳ καὶ πολλοὺς αὐτῶν ἐν τῷ κινδύνῳ διέφθειραν. ἐν ᾧ καιρῷ προσφιλονικήσαντες πρὸς τὸ γεγονὸς ἐλάττωμʼ αὐτοῖς Ῥωμαῖοι μετʼ ὀλίγας ἡμέρας ἐξῆλθον καὶ συμβαλόντες πᾶσι τοῖς στρατοπέδοις ἐν τῇ τῶν Σεντινατῶν χώρᾳ πρὸς τοὺς προειρημένους τοὺς μὲν πλείστους ἀπέκτειναν, τοὺς δὲ λοιποὺς ἠνάγκασαν προτροπάδην ἑκάστους εἰς τὴν οἰκείαν φυγεῖν.
quote.en: After this, in the fourth year, Samnites and Gauls made common cause, drew up against the Romans in the land of the Camertes and killed many of them in the battle. The Romans, their will to win roused by the defeat they had suffered, marched out a few days later and, engaging with all their legions in the land of the Sentinates against the same enemy, killed most of them and forced the rest to flee headlong, each to his own country.
quote.it: Dopo questi fatti, di nuovo nel quarto anno, Sanniti e Galli, messisi d'accordo, si schierarono contro i Romani nel territorio dei Camerti e ne uccisero molti nello scontro. Allora i Romani, punti dalla sconfitta subita, uscirono pochi giorni dopo e, scontratisi con tutte le legioni nel territorio dei Sentinati contro i predetti, ne uccisero la maggior parte e costrinsero gli altri a fuggire precipitosamente ciascuno nella propria terra.

blocks.note: Perseus text, with line breaks closed up. English and Italian ours.

blocks.text: The accounts differ on three points. The place: Clusium in Livy, the land of the Camertes in Polybius. The enemy and the result: Senones who destroy the legion, or Umbrians who are beaten in the end, in Livy; Samnites and Gauls together, victorious, in Polybius. The interval: Polybius puts Sentinum a few days later, while Livy gives no count of days.

Pleiades places Clusium at Chiusi in Etruria and Camerinum at Camerino, an Umbrian town on the borders of Picenum, allied to Rome from 309 BC. Whether Livy's remark that Clusium was once called Camars has anything to do with Polybius' Camertes, nothing opened for this scene says.
blocks.note: No modern study of the question was opened.

blocks.text: Decius had told the pontifex M. Livius, as he went down into the line, not to leave his side. He ordered him to dictate the words by which he would devote himself and the legions of the enemy for the army of the Roman people. Livy says the prayer and the dress were those his father had used at the Veseris in the Latin war.

For the father, Livy gives the procedure. The pontifex bade him put on the toga praetexta, veil his head, put a hand out under the toga to touch his chin, and stand on a spear laid under his feet. The prayer names Janus, Jupiter, Mars pater, Quirinus, Bellona, the Lares, the di Novensiles and Indigetes, the gods who have power over us and the enemy, and the di Manes, and ends by devoting the enemy's legions and auxiliaries with himself to the di Manes and Tellus. He then girt himself in the cinctus Gabinus and rode armed into the enemy.
To the customary prayers the son, in Livy, added his own curses.

quote.la: prae se agere sese formidinem ac fugam caedemque ac cruorem, caelestium inferorum iras, contacturum funebribus diris signa tela arma hostium, locumque eundem suae pestis ac Gallorum ac Samnitium fore
quote.en: that he drove before him dread and flight, slaughter and blood, the wrath of the gods above and below; that he would taint the standards, weapons and arms of the enemy with deadly curses; and that the same place would see his own destruction and that of the Gauls and Samnites.
quote.it: che spingeva davanti a sé terrore e fuga, strage e sangue, le ire degli dèi celesti e inferi; che avrebbe contaminato con funeste maledizioni le insegne, i dardi e le armi dei nemici; e che lo stesso luogo sarebbe stato quello della rovina sua e dei Galli e dei Sanniti.

blocks.note: Reported speech in Livy. 'contacturum' is a correction; the apparatus gives the manuscripts' reading as 'contracturum'. The apparatus note is removed from the Perseus text.

blocks.text: Decius had handed his lictors to Livius and ordered him to act pro praetore. After the consul fell, the pontifex shouted that the Romans had won, released by the consul's fate, and that Gauls and Samnites now belonged to Tellus and the di Manes.

The body could not be found that day, buried under heaps of Gauls. It was found the next day and brought back, and Fabius gave his colleague his funeral. In the triumph the soldiers' rough songs celebrated the death of Decius as much as the victory of Fabius.

cards.title: Chariots, and javelins picked off the ground

blocks.text: Livy calls the Gallic vehicles esseda and carri: an armed enemy standing on them came on with a great noise of horses and wheels, a kind of fighting new to the Romans, and it was the noise their horses could not bear. The writers he rejects counted a thousand carpenta.

The Roman horse had been carried in among the Gallic foot when the chariots came: the Oxford text prints peditum, Madvig's correction of the manuscripts' equitum. Roberts' English has them among the enemy's cavalry, which is what the manuscripts say.

When the Gauls stood packed behind their shields and a fight at close quarters looked hard, the legates had the pila that lay strewn between the lines gathered and thrown into the shield-wall. Most stuck in shields and few in bodies, yet the mass went down, many falling stunned and unwounded.

The word 'few' is partly an editor's. The main manuscripts give uerarisque rutis, others uerutis or uerrutis. Hertz kept rarisque and cut the rest; the Oxford text and Weissenborn–Müller print that. The Oxford apparatus adds its editors' own suggestion verutisque raris and Drakenborch's rarisque verutis, either of which would put light javelins, veruta, among the missiles.

A few lines later the Gauls are again standing packed in a testudo when the Campanian horse is sent round them. Roberts thought this hard to square with the collapse just described: perhaps only the front rank had fallen, or a copyist repeated the sentence.

cards.title: Eighty-two asses, a cloak and a tunic

blocks.text: What Fabius' soldiers took home from the triumph:

quote.la: data ex praeda militibus aeris octogeni bini sagaque et tunicae, praemia illa tempestate militiae haudquaquam spernenda.
quote.en: Out of the booty the soldiers were given eighty-two asses each, and cloaks and tunics, rewards of service by no means to be despised in those days.
quote.it: Dal bottino furono dati ai soldati ottantadue assi a testa, e saghi e tuniche, premi del servizio militare per quei tempi tutt'altro che disprezzabili.

blocks.note: Livy writes 'aeris octogeni bini', eighty-two of bronze each. The English is ours.

blocks.text: Later in the year Fabius killed 4,500 men of Perusia and took about 1,740, who were ransomed at 310 of bronze a head; all the other plunder went to the soldiers. The figures are Livy's. One Perusine prisoner was priced at nearly four times a soldier's share in bronze from Sentinum.
blocks.note: The comparison (310 against 82) is our arithmetic.

blocks.text: The other side offered money too. The Gallic auxiliaries were solicited for pay, and the report that reached Rome the year before spoke of a huge price. Who found the money, and in what form, Livy does not say at either place.

Pleiades places Sentinum near Sassoferrato, in what is now the Marche. Livy never names the town in his account of the battle, only its territory, the ager Sentinas, beyond the Apennines for an army coming from Rome.

Of the ground he gives little. The camps lay about four miles apart. Both armies went down into a plain, and the hind was driven by the wolf out of the mountains and ran across the fields between the two lines. He names no river and no hill, and does not say which way either army faced.
Pleiades describes the ager Gallicus, the region of Gallic settlement to the north, as territory captured by Rome following the battle of Sentinum. Livy's account of 295 records no annexation.
blocks.note: The Pleiades description is a modern summary; no ancient passage for the annexation was opened.

blocks.text: The Samnites were a long way from home. Livy has a column of five thousand make its way back through the land of the Paeligni, who surrounded it and killed about a thousand.
